content: Bisulfide, also known as hydrosulfide, is the anion with the chemical formula HS−, though it is often written as SH−. This anion is the conjugate base of hydrogen sulfide (H2S). In aqueous solutions, the dominant species depends on the pH of the solution. When the pH is less than 7 (acidic conditions), hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is the predominant species. However, when the pH is greater than 7 (alkaline conditions), bisulfide (HS−) becomes the dominant species. Various salts of bisulfide are well-documented, including sodium hydrosulfide (NaHS), potassium hydrosulfide (KHS), and ammonium hydrosulfide (NH4HS). Some compounds that are described as salts of the sulfide dianion (S2−) are, in fact, primarily composed of hydrosulfide (HS−). For instance, the hydrated form of sodium sulfide, which is nominally represented by the formula Na2S·(H2O)9, is more accurately described as NaSH·NaOH·(H2O)8. In the ultraviolet-visible (UV/VIS) spectrum, aqueous bisulfide exhibits light absorption at approximately 230 nm. It is important to note that bisulfide (HS−) is sometimes mistakenly confused with the disulfide dianion (S22−), which is a chemically distinct species.
